query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The application of a 10 μm thick Al2O3 coating on ZrB2-based ceramic components will improve their resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion by reducing the reaction between the aluminum and the ZrB2, resulting in a 30% reduction in corrosion rate compared to uncoated ZrB2.
generation.intervention: Surface modification with a 10 μm thick Al2O3 coating
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a stable Al2O3 layer
generation.mechanism: The Al2O3 coating acts as a barrier to molten aluminum penetration, reducing corrosion by preventing direct contact between the ZrB2 and the aluminum
generation.predicted_outcome: A 30% reduction in corrosion rate compared to uncoated ZrB2
generation.boundary: The Al2O3 coating remains effective as long as it adheres well to the ZrB2 substrate and does not crack during thermal cycling
generation.uncertainty: The actual reduction in corrosion rate may vary depending on the optimization of the coating thickness and deposition method

falsification_experiment.design: Compare the corrosion rates of coated and uncoated ZrB2 samples in molten aluminum at 700°C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the corrosion rate of the coated sample is not significantly lower than that of the uncoated sample, the hypothesis is falsified
